text: Group by gave us one row per category. But often you only want the groups that pass a test: industries with more than ten accounts, or emails that appear more than once. WHERE can't do that. HAVING can.

GROUP BY Industry builds one row per industry. Then HAVING COUNT of Id greater than ten keeps only the groups above ten. Same division of labor as T-SQL: WHERE decides which rows go into the groups, and HAVING decides which groups survive.

Read it in execution order. WHERE narrows to this year's close dates. GROUP BY builds one row per stage. HAVING keeps stages over a million dollars with at least three deals. ORDER BY sorts what's left. Put any condition without an aggregate in WHERE, since it runs earlier and leaves the groups less to process.

Here is a classic real-world use. Group contacts by email, and keep groups with a count above one. Every duplicated email comes back with its count. The WHERE Email not equals null matters: without it, every contact with no email forms one giant null group that swamps the results.

Inside HAVING you can use aggregate functions and grouped fields. Repeat the aggregate in full, don't expect to reuse the alias. Combine conditions with AND, OR, and parentheses. But you can't use an ungrouped plain field, because after grouping it no longer has one value per group.
Now you can summarize, group, and filter groups. Next up: Lesson 10, date functions in SOQL, so you can group and filter by year, quarter, and month.
